summary:
The Republic of Karelia stands under the national framework of Russia, which sets the risk any transgender visitor carries. A 2023 law signed by President Vladimir Putin prohibits gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, banning legal gender recognition and effectively ending trans-specific healthcare; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises public expression that includes, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition. Same-sex marriage is unavailable and no discrimination protection covers LGBT+ people.

Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and national government warnings expressly advise LGBT travellers of that exposure. The US State Department's travel advisory advises against all travel to Russia regardless of any personal characteristic, citing the risk of wrongful detention and arbitrary law enforcement.

Enforcement since the extremist designation is documented at scale. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions, 98 administrative and three criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols; at least 20 people faced criminal charges from January 2024, three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years, and repeated display of banned symbols carries up to four years in prison. Cases under the propaganda statutes have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines bringing more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in two years. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling in January 2024, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, ordering about 100 patrons at one venue to face walls for search and photography, with at least two other venues raided the same night.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records the national framework this republic stands under and assesses that trans people, public LGBT+ advocates and people in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, while LGB people are not generally at real risk solely on the basis of sexual orientation. The same note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention. It records 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024 and contains no division-specific facts on Karelia.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented: a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.
tangentialFactors:
The risk profile in Karelia is set by national designations rather than by regional policy: the Supreme Court's extremist ruling and the expanded propaganda statute apply uniformly, and raids in the two largest cities within 48 hours of that ruling indicate how quickly measures of that kind are operationalised elsewhere in the country.

Country-level assessments differ in their threshold. The UK Home Office notes that LGB people are not generally at risk of persecution solely for sexual orientation, but separates out trans people as a category likely to face persecution; the US State Department advises against all travel without any carve-out for particular characteristics. Visitors who rely on a sexual-orientation-only reading of travel guidance will understate the exposure that attaches specifically to gender identity.

Conditions in the North Caucasus, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, are treated as materially worse than the national baseline, and the UK Home Office note names the region alongside trans people and public advocates in its persecution finding.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming surgery are prohibited for residents as well as visitors under the 2023 statute, and trans-specific healthcare has been effectively unavailable since then. Same-sex marriage is not available and there is no statutory discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Residents face the same extremism exposure as visitors, and the bulk of the 101 convictions recorded to June 2025 were administrative rather than criminal, indicating routine low-level processing as well as prosecutions carrying long sentences. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to people fleeing Russia.

The UK Home Office treats LGBT+ people, including those in Chechnya, as a particular social group for the purpose of refugee-convention claims, and its assessment that trans people are likely to face persecution-forming treatment sets the standard for UK asylum determinations.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Karelia-specific legal or enforcement facts appear in the source inventory: the UK Home Office note explicitly contains no division-specific material, and none of the cited raids, deaths or prosecutions occurred in this republic. Whether the Karelian authorities have issued regional directives on LGBT+ assembly, venues or policing is unresolved and not sourced here.

Regional variation in enforcement practice within Russia is not documented in these sources; the inventory records national statutes, national designations and incidents in other cities, so the degree to which Karelia's courts or police diverge from the national pattern remains unresolved.

Figures on impacted individuals cover Russia as a whole for 2022 to 2024; no breakdown by republic or by the share of cases involving transgender respondents is available in the inventory.
